text: You've now covered why GPUs are fast, why their memory is the real constraint, and what the actual instance families on Azure and AWS are built for. This last lesson puts it together into a decision you'll make constantly as a cloud architect: does this workload actually need a GPU, or not.

The real test isn't whether a project is labeled AI or machine learning. It's whether the dominant computational cost is a large, parallelizable matrix or tensor operation — the exact thing Lesson 1 showed GPU cores are built to accelerate. If the answer is yes, a GPU is likely justified. If the answer is no, start with CPU and make the case for GPU from there, not the other way around.

Some workloads genuinely pass that test. Training a real deep learning model of any real size — dense layers, convolutions, transformer attention, all dominated by matmul. Fine-tuning a large model, which stays GPU-only even once you're leaning on LoRA or quantization to make it fit in memory. And high-throughput inference serving, at the batch sizes and concurrency where GPU parallelism is actually being exercised rather than sitting idle.

Plenty of AI-adjacent work doesn't pass, though. Traditional ETL — filtering, joining, aggregating rows — is branchy and I/O-bound, and a GPU's thousands of simple cores add nothing to a WHERE clause. Classical ML on tabular data, like gradient-boosted trees or logistic regression, usually runs just as well or better on CPU at realistic dataset sizes. And a small model serving a handful of requests per second simply doesn't generate enough sustained load to keep a GPU's cores busy.

Run through a short checklist before provisioning: is the cost dominated by large parallelizable matmul? Does it actually fit the memory math from Lesson 2 on a real instance, or does it need LoRA, quantization, or multi-GPU sharding? Is it single-node or does it need the multi-node interconnect from Lesson 3? And is there enough sustained volume to keep the GPU busy? Get this wrong in either direction — forcing GPU where it isn't needed, or forcing a large job onto CPU to save cost — and you pay for it, either in idle GPU-hours or in weeks of extra wall-clock time.

That closes out GPU computing fundamentals. You now have the vocabulary and the judgment to reason about any GPU provisioning decision from first principles, rather than defaulting to 'AI means GPU' — which is exactly the foundation the rest of this course builds on.
